etymology: From Greek oikonomia (household management, administration, dispensation). The Trinity considered in the works of God toward creation — the distinct roles of Father, Son, and Spirit in creation, redemption, and the application of salvation. Distinguished from (but inseparable from) the ontological / immanent Trinity (God as He is in Himself).
biblical_def: From Greek oikonomia (administration, dispensation); the Trinity considered in the works of God toward creation — the distinct but harmonious roles of Father, Son, and Spirit in the divine economy of creation, providence, redemption, and the application of salvation. The economic Trinity describes the outward operations (opera ad extra) of the triune God: the Father plans and sends; the Son accomplishes redemption; the Spirit applies it. In creation, the Father creates through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16) by the Spirit (Genesis 1:2). In redemption, the Father sends the Son (John 3:16; Galatians 4:4), the Son accomplishes the atonement (Hebrews 9:14), and the Spirit applies it to the elect (Titus 3:5-6; 1 Peter 1:2, the elect through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, displaying all three Persons). The economic Trinity is distinguished from (but inseparable from) the ontological / immanent Trinity (God as He is in Himself, the eternal relations of the Persons). The Reformed-confessional principle holds that the outward works of the Trinity are undivided (opera Trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt) — all three Persons act in every external work — while the works are appropriated distinctly to the Persons according to their eternal relations (creation appropriated to the Father, redemption to the Son, sanctification to the Spirit). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the economic Trinity reveals the immanent Trinity (the roles in the economy correspond to and reveal the eternal relations) without collapsing into it; the distinct roles of the Persons in the work of salvation display the one God who is Father, Son, and Spirit, working harmoniously for the redemption of His people and the glory of His name.
webster_summary: From Greek oikonomia; the Trinity in the works of God toward creation — the distinct roles of Father (plans, sends), Son (accomplishes redemption), Spirit (applies it); distinguished from but inseparable from the ontological/immanent Trinity; the outward works undivided yet distinctly appropriated.
webster_full: ECONOMIC TRINITY, n. phr. (Trinitarian theology; Greek oikonomia, administration) The Trinity in the works of God toward creation — the distinct, harmonious roles of Father, Son, and Spirit in creation, providence, redemption, and the application of salvation (the opera ad extra). The Father plans and sends; the Son accomplishes redemption; the Spirit applies it (1 Peter 1:2; Titus 3:5-6; John 3:16; Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 9:14). Distinguished from but inseparable from the ontological/immanent Trinity (God as He is in Himself). The outward works of the Trinity are undivided (opera Trinitatis ad extra indivisa sunt) yet distinctly appropriated to the Persons according to their eternal relations. The economic Trinity reveals the immanent Trinity without collapsing into it.

corruption_summary: The economic Trinity must be distinguished from but held inseparable with the immanent Trinity; the corruption is to collapse the economic into the immanent (subordinationism, deriving eternal subordination from economic roles) or to sever them (denying that the economy reveals the immanent relations).
corruption_paragraphs: The economic Trinity must be carefully distinguished from but held inseparable with the immanent / ontological Trinity. One corruption collapses the economic into the immanent, deriving an eternal ontological subordination of the Son from His economic role of being sent and obeying (the error of the eternal-functional-subordination debate); this risks compromising the equality of the Persons. The opposite corruption severs the economic from the immanent, denying that the economy truly reveals the eternal relations (so that the God revealed in the economy of salvation might not be the God as He truly is in Himself). The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds the substantive balance: the economic Trinity (the roles in the work of salvation) truly reveals the immanent Trinity (the eternal relations of the Persons) — the Son who is sent in the economy is the Son who is eternally begotten of the Father; the Spirit who is sent is the Spirit who eternally proceeds — without the economic roles implying any inequality or subordination of essence among the co-equal Persons. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the distinct economic roles of Father, Son, and Spirit display the one triune God working harmoniously for the redemption of His people, and reveal the eternal relations of the co-equal, co-eternal Persons.

etymology: From Greek ontos (being) + logos (study). The Trinity considered as God is in Himself — the one divine essence subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) in their eternal relations. Also called the immanent or essential Trinity. Distinguished from the economic Trinity (the works toward creation).
biblical_def: From Greek ontos (being); the Trinity considered as God is in Himself, apart from His works toward creation — the one divine essence subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) in their eternal relations. Also called the immanent Trinity or the essential Trinity. The ontological Trinity describes God's eternal inner life: the one undivided divine essence (the three Persons share the one indivisible Godhead, homoousios, of one substance); the three distinct Persons (the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, distinguished by their personal properties and relations, not by any division of essence); and the eternal relations of origin (the Father unbegotten; the Son eternally begotten of the Father, eternal generation; the Spirit eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son, eternal procession). The ontological Trinity is the foundation: God is eternally and necessarily triune, independent of creation; He would be triune even if He had never created. The doctrine is grounded in the biblical revelation of the three Persons as fully and equally God (the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God) yet one God (Deuteronomy 6:4, the LORD is one), and in the eternal relations revealed in Scripture (the Son eternally with the Father, John 1:1; 17:5, 24; the eternal love of the Father for the Son, John 17:24). The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession II.3; the Nicene-Constantinopolitan and Athanasian Creeds) holds the substantive ontological Trinity. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine against the modalist denial (which denies the real distinction of the Persons), the subordinationist and Arian denial (which denies the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons), and the tritheist error (which divides the one essence into three gods). The ontological Trinity is the eternal reality of the one God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the foundation of the economic Trinity revealed in the works of salvation.
webster_summary: The Trinity considered as God is in Himself — the one divine essence subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons in their eternal relations (Father unbegotten, Son eternally begotten, Spirit eternally proceeding); also the immanent/essential Trinity; distinguished from the economic Trinity; God eternally and necessarily triune.
webster_full: ONTOLOGICAL TRINITY, n. phr. (Trinitarian theology; Greek ontos, being) The Trinity as God is in Himself, apart from His works — the one divine essence subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) in their eternal relations. Also the immanent or essential Trinity. The one undivided essence (the Persons homoousios, of one substance); three distinct Persons (distinguished by personal properties and relations, not division of essence); eternal relations of origin (Father unbegotten; Son eternally begotten; Spirit eternally proceeding). God eternally and necessarily triune, independent of creation. Westminster II.3; the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds. Held against modalism, subordinationism/Arianism, and tritheism.

corruption_summary: The ontological Trinity is held against modalism (denying the real distinction of Persons), subordinationism/Arianism (denying co-equality and co-eternity), and tritheism (dividing the one essence into three gods); God is one essence in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons.
corruption_paragraphs: The ontological Trinity is held against three classic errors. Modalism (Sabellianism) denies the real eternal distinction of the Persons, treating Father, Son, and Spirit as three modes or manifestations of the one God rather than three distinct Persons; this contradicts the biblical revelation of the Persons in real relation to one another (the Father loving the Son, John 17:24; the Son praying to the Father, John 17; the Spirit sent by the Father and the Son). Subordinationism and Arianism deny the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons, making the Son (and Spirit) lesser or created beings; this contradicts the biblical revelation of the full deity of the Son (John 1:1; 20:28) and the Spirit, and was condemned at Nicaea (the Son homoousios, of one substance with the Father). Tritheism divides the one divine essence into three gods; this contradicts the biblical revelation that the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene-confessional doctrine: one God, one undivided divine essence, subsisting in three co-equal, co-eternal Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), distinguished by their eternal relations (the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit eternally proceeding) but not divided in essence. God is eternally and necessarily triune; the ontological Trinity is the eternal reality of the one God revealed in the economy of salvation.

etymology: From Greek kenoo (to empty), from Philippians 2:7 (made himself of no reputation, literally emptied himself). The orthodox doctrine concerns what the Son's self-emptying in the incarnation rightly means; distinguished from the heterodox kenotic theory (that the Son divested Himself of divine attributes in becoming man).
biblical_def: From Greek kenoo (to empty), drawn from Philippians 2:7, where Christ made himself of no reputation (literally emptied himself, heauton ekenosen) in taking the form of a servant. The doctrine concerns the right interpretation of the Son's self-emptying in the incarnation, and the term must be carefully distinguished between its orthodox sense and the heterodox kenotic theory. The orthodox doctrine of the kenosis holds that the Son's self-emptying consisted not in the laying aside of His divine attributes or deity, but in the veiling of His glory and the taking on of the form of a servant — the addition of a true human nature, the assumption of the lowly condition of humanity, the voluntary submission to the humiliation of incarnate life and ultimately the cross. The Son did not cease to be God or divest Himself of any divine attribute; rather, the eternal Son, remaining fully God, took to Himself a full human nature and the lowly estate of a servant, veiling His divine glory and humbling Himself unto death (Philippians 2:6-8). The heterodox kenotic theory (developed in 19th-century German and British theology — Thomasius, Gess, and others) holds that the Son actually divested Himself of His divine attributes (or of the relative attributes such as omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) in becoming man, so that the incarnate Christ was not fully God during His earthly life. This is rejected by orthodox and Reformed theology as compromising the full deity of the incarnate Christ and the immutability of God (God cannot cease to be God or lay aside His essential attributes). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine of the kenosis: the Son emptied Himself not by subtraction (divesting deity or divine attributes) but by addition and humiliation (adding a true human nature, taking the form of a servant, veiling His glory, humbling Himself unto death); the incarnate Christ remained fully and unchangeably God while also becoming fully man, in the one Person, two natures, of the hypostatic union.
webster_summary: From Greek kenoo (to empty); Philippians 2:7 (made himself of no reputation); the orthodox doctrine holds the Son emptied Himself by addition and humiliation (taking a human nature, the form of a servant, veiling His glory), not by divesting deity or divine attributes; rejects the heterodox kenotic theory.
webster_full: KENOSIS (DOCTRINE), n. (Christology; Greek kenoo, to empty; Philippians 2:7, heauton ekenosen, emptied himself) The orthodox doctrine: the Son's self-emptying consisted not in laying aside His deity or divine attributes, but in veiling His glory and taking the form of a servant — the addition of a true human nature, the assumption of the lowly condition of humanity, submission to humiliation and the cross (Philippians 2:6-8). The Son remained fully God. The heterodox kenotic theory (19th-c. Thomasius, Gess) holds the Son divested His divine attributes in becoming man, so the incarnate Christ was not fully God; rejected as compromising Christ's full deity and God's immutability. Emptying by addition and humiliation, not subtraction of deity.

corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of the kenosis requires careful distinction between the orthodox sense and the heterodox kenotic theory. The heterodox kenotic theory (developed in 19th-century German theology by Thomasius, Gess, and others, and influential in some British theology) holds that the Son actually divested Himself of His divine attributes (or at least the relative attributes — omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) in becoming man, so that during His earthly life the incarnate Christ was not fully God. This is rejected by orthodox and Reformed theology on substantive grounds: it compromises the full deity of the incarnate Christ (in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, Colossians 2:9); it contradicts the immutability of God (God cannot cease to be God or lay aside His essential attributes, for the divine attributes are not separable from the divine essence); and it undermines the hypostatic union (the incarnate Christ must be fully God and fully man in the one Person). The orthodox doctrine of the kenosis holds that the Son emptied Himself not by subtraction but by addition and humiliation: He did not lay aside His deity or divine attributes; rather, the eternal Son, remaining fully and unchangeably God, took to Himself a full human nature, assumed the form of a servant and the lowly estate of incarnate humanity, veiled His divine glory, and humbled Himself unto death (Philippians 2:6-8). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine: Christ emptied Himself by adding humanity and humbling Himself, not by divesting deity; the incarnate Christ remained fully God while becoming fully man.

etymology: The orthodox Christological doctrine, defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451), that the one Person of Christ subsists in two natures — fully divine and fully human — united without confusion, change, division, or separation. Foundational to the hypostatic union.
biblical_def: The orthodox Christological doctrine that the one Person of Christ subsists in two complete natures — a fully divine nature and a fully human nature — united in the one Person without confusion, change, division, or separation. The doctrine was definitively formulated at the Council of Chalcedon (451) against the Christological heresies, in the Chalcedonian Definition: Christ is truly God and truly man... consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead, and consubstantial with us according to the manhood; in all things like unto us, without sin... to be acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably; the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person. The biblical foundation is the consistent witness to both the full deity and the full humanity of Christ in the one Person. Full deity: the Word was God (John 1:1); in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Colossians 2:9); He is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of His person (Hebrews 1:3); Thomas confesses Him my Lord and my God (John 20:28). Full humanity: the Word was made flesh (John 1:14); He was born of a woman (Galatians 4:4); He grew in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:52); He hungered, thirsted, wearied, wept, suffered, and died (a true body and a reasonable soul); He was tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). The two natures are united in the one Person (not two persons; the heresy of Nestorianism) without being mixed or confused into a third hybrid nature (the heresy of Eutychianism / monophysitism), without the divine nature being changed, and without the natures being divided or separated. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Chalcedonian doctrine: Christ is one Person in two natures, fully God and fully man, the God-man (theanthropos), the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5).

webster_full: TWO NATURES OF CHRIST, n. phr. (Christology) The one Person of Christ subsists in two complete natures — fully divine and fully human — united without confusion, change, division, or separation. Defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451): Christ truly God and truly man... to be acknowledged in two natures, inconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably; the distinction of natures being by no means taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, and concurring in one Person. Full deity (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9; Hebrews 1:3; John 20:28) and full humanity (John 1:14; Galatians 4:4; Luke 2:52; Hebrews 4:15) in the one Person. Held against Nestorianism (two persons), Eutychianism/monophysitism (mixed nature), and the denials of either nature.

corruption_summary: The two natures of Christ are held against Nestorianism (dividing into two persons), Eutychianism/monophysitism (mixing into one hybrid nature), and the denials of either the full deity or the full humanity; Chalcedon defines two natures in one Person without confusion, change, division, or separation.
corruption_paragraphs: The two-natures doctrine is held against the classic Christological heresies, each of which the Chalcedonian Definition addresses. Arianism denied the full deity of Christ (making the Son a created being); rejected by Nicaea (the Son homoousios with the Father). Apollinarianism denied the full humanity of Christ (holding that the divine Logos replaced the human soul/mind in Christ); rejected, for Christ must have a complete human nature (body and reasonable soul) to redeem the whole man. Nestorianism so divided the two natures as to imply two persons (or a merely moral union of two persons); rejected, for Christ is one Person. Eutychianism / monophysitism so mixed the two natures as to produce one hybrid nature (the human nature absorbed into or blended with the divine); rejected, for the two natures remain distinct, the property of each preserved. The Chalcedonian Definition holds the substantive orthodox doctrine with its famous four adverbs: the two natures united without confusion, without change, without division, without separation in the one Person. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Chalcedonian Christology: Christ is one Person (the eternal Son) subsisting in two complete natures, fully God and fully man; this is the foundation of His mediatorial work (as God, He has infinite worth to satisfy divine justice; as man, He stands in the place of men) and the heart of the gospel (the God-man who alone could reconcile God and men, 1 Timothy 2:5).

etymology: The threefold office (munus triplex) of Christ: He executes the offices of a prophet (revealing God and His will), a priest (offering Himself as sacrifice and interceding), and a king (ruling and defending His people and subduing His enemies). Systematized by Calvin (Institutes II.15) and the Reformed confessions (Heidelberg Q. 31; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 23-26).
biblical_def: The threefold office (munus triplex) of Christ, by which He executes the work of redemption in the three mediatorial offices of prophet, priest, and king. The doctrine was systematized by Calvin (Institutes II.15) and codified in the Reformed confessions (Heidelberg Catechism Q. 31; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 23-26; Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 42-45). The three offices, anointed in the OT (prophets, priests, and kings were anointed; Christ is the Anointed One, the Messiah / Christ, who unites all three offices). (1) Christ as Prophet: He reveals to us, by His Word and Spirit, the whole will of God for our salvation (Deuteronomy 18:15, the prophet like Moses; Acts 3:22; Christ as the Word, John 1:1, 18; the one who declares the Father, John 1:18; the great teacher and revealer of God). (2) Christ as Priest: He once offered Himself a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice and reconcile us to God, and He continually intercedes for us (Hebrews 7-10; the great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek; the once-for-all sacrifice, Hebrews 9:26; 10:12; the continual intercession, Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). (3) Christ as King: He subdues us to Himself, rules and defends us, and restrains and conquers all His and our enemies (Psalm 2; the King enthroned at the Father's right hand, Ephesians 1:20-22; Philippians 2:9-11; the reigning Christ who must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25). The threefold office corresponds to the comprehensive work of redemption: as Prophet, Christ addresses our ignorance (revealing God); as Priest, our guilt (atoning and interceding); as King, our bondage (subduing, ruling, and defending). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the threefold office as a comprehensive framework for Christ's mediatorial work, and notes its application: the believer, united to Christ, shares in His anointing (the believer a prophet, priest, and king in derivative measure, 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6, kings and priests unto God); and the threefold office of Christ shapes the believer's response — receiving Christ's prophetic Word, resting in His priestly atonement and intercession, and submitting to His kingly rule.

webster_full: PROPHET, PRIEST, AND KING, n. phr. (Christology) The threefold office (munus triplex) of Christ. Systematized by Calvin (Institutes II.15); Heidelberg Q. 31; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 23-26. (1) Prophet: reveals the whole will of God for our salvation (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22; John 1:18). (2) Priest: once offered Himself a sacrifice to satisfy justice and reconcile us, and continually intercedes (Hebrews 7-10; 7:25; Romans 8:34). (3) King: subdues us to Himself, rules and defends us, restrains and conquers His and our enemies (Psalm 2; Ephesians 1:20-22; 1 Corinthians 15:25). Corresponds to our ignorance (Prophet), guilt (Priest), bondage (King). The believer, united to Christ, shares derivatively in His anointing (1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6).

corruption_summary: The threefold office is the comprehensive framework for Christ's mediatorial work; the principal mishandling is the truncation that emphasizes one office (often the priestly) while neglecting the prophetic and kingly, producing an incomplete Christology.
corruption_paragraphs: Prophet, priest, and king as a doctrine does not undergo lexical corruption. The principal mishandling is the truncation that emphasizes one office while neglecting the others, producing an incomplete Christology. Some traditions emphasize Christ's priestly office (the atonement and intercession) almost to the exclusion of His prophetic and kingly offices, producing a Christ who saves from guilt but is not received as the revealer of God's will (Prophet) or submitted to as the ruling Lord (King). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the threefold office in its fulness: Christ is Prophet, Priest, and King, addressing the whole of our need (our ignorance by His prophetic revealing, our guilt by His priestly atonement and intercession, our bondage by His kingly subduing, ruling, and defending). The threefold office shapes the believer's whole response to Christ: he receives Christ's prophetic Word (submitting his mind to Christ's revelation), rests in Christ's priestly work (trusting the once-for-all atonement and the continual intercession), and submits to Christ's kingly rule (obeying the Lord who reigns over all). The kingly office in particular is often neglected in soft-evangelical Christology that wants a Savior but not a Lord; the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the full kingship of Christ, who reigns at the Father's right hand and must reign till He has put all enemies under His feet (1 Corinthians 15:25), and to whose kingly rule the whole of life, household, church, and civil order is subject.

etymology: From Greek theos (God) + anthropos (man); the God-man. The technical Christological term for the incarnate Christ, the one Person who is both fully God and fully man, uniting the divine and human natures in the hypostatic union.
biblical_def: From Greek theos (God) + anthropos (man); the God-man, the technical Christological term for the incarnate Christ as the one Person who is both fully God and fully man. The term expresses the heart of orthodox Christology: in the incarnation, the eternal Son of God (the second Person of the Trinity) took to Himself a complete human nature, so that the one Person of Christ is at once fully divine and fully human — the God-man, theanthropos. The term is not found verbatim in Scripture but expresses the biblical revelation of the incarnate Christ. The biblical foundation: the Word who was God was made flesh (John 1:1, 14); in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Colossians 2:9); He is God manifest in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16); He is Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23); the child born is the mighty God (Isaiah 9:6); He is the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), who as God-man uniquely bridges the infinite gulf between God and fallen men. The theanthropos doctrine grounds the sufficiency of Christ's mediatorial work: only the God-man could accomplish redemption — as man, He could stand in the place of men, take their nature, bear their guilt, and die in their stead; as God, His one sacrifice had infinite worth to satisfy the infinite justice of God and to redeem a countless multitude. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the theanthropos: the incarnate Christ is the God-man, fully God and fully man in the one Person, the unique and all-sufficient Mediator; this is the marvel and mystery at the heart of the gospel (1 Timothy 3:16, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh), and the foundation of the believer's salvation.

Grounds the sufficiency of His mediatorial work: as man He stands in men's place; as God His sacrifice has infinite worth. The marvel at the heart of the gospel.

corruption_paragraphs: Theanthropos as a Christological term does not undergo lexical corruption. The doctrine it expresses (the God-man, fully God and fully man in one Person) is held against the denials of either nature. The denials of the full deity (Arianism, and modern liberal Christologies that treat Christ as merely a great man or moral teacher) contradict the biblical revelation that the Word was God (John 1:1) and that all the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Him bodily (Colossians 2:9). The denials of the full humanity (Docetism, which held that Christ only appeared to have a human body; Apollinarianism, which held that the divine Logos replaced the human soul in Christ) contradict the biblical revelation that the Word was made flesh (John 1:14) and that Christ was made like His brethren in all things, tempted like as we are yet without sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15). This is the marvel and mystery at the heart of the gospel (1 Timothy 3:16, God was manifest in the flesh) and the foundation of the believer's salvation: only the God-man could bridge the gulf between God and fallen men, taking our nature to stand in our place and possessing infinite divine worth to satisfy divine justice. The God-man is the wonder of redemption, the eternal Son who became what He was not (man) without ceasing to be what He was (God), for the salvation of His people.

etymology: Latin: the Calvinistic beyond (a term coined by Lutheran opponents). The Reformed Christological doctrine that the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within the human nature — the Son continued to fill and uphold the universe even while incarnate (the Son existing also beyond or outside the flesh, etiam extra carnem).
biblical_def: Latin for the Calvinistic beyond / outside (a term coined by Lutheran opponents in the Reformed-Lutheran Christological controversies); the Reformed Christological doctrine that the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within or exhausted by the human nature. The doctrine holds that the eternal Son, while truly and personally united to the human nature in the incarnation, continued to exist and act also beyond (extra) the human nature — continuing to fill heaven and earth, to uphold all things by the word of His power, to be omnipresent according to His divine nature — even during His incarnate life on earth. The Son was not so confined within the human body that He ceased His cosmic divine operations; the infinite divine nature is not contained or circumscribed by the finite human nature. The doctrine is grounded in: (1) the immensity and omnipresence of the divine nature, which cannot be confined to one location (Jeremiah 23:24; the divine nature fills heaven and earth); (2) Colossians 1:17, by him all things consist (the Son upholds the universe, a cosmic operation that did not cease during the incarnation); (3) John 3:13, the Son of man which is in heaven (the Son of Man spoken of as in heaven even while on earth, in the Person who unites the two natures); (4) Hebrews 1:3, the Son upholding all things by the word of His power. Though called the extra Calvinisticum by Lutheran opponents (who, holding the ubiquity of Christ's body for their consubstantiation doctrine, objected to it), the doctrine is in fact the catholic Christological position held by the Fathers (Athanasius, Augustine, Cyril) and the medieval theologians, not a Calvinist innovation. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was truly and personally united to the human nature without being confined within it; even while incarnate, He continued to fill and uphold the universe according to His divine nature. The doctrine preserves the integrity of both natures (the infinite divine nature not confined by the finite human nature; the finite human nature not made omnipresent) and undergirds the Reformed spiritual-presence doctrine of the Lord's Supper (against the Lutheran ubiquity-of-Christ's-body).
webster_summary: Latin the Calvinistic beyond (coined by Lutheran opponents); the Reformed Christological doctrine that the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within the human nature, continuing to fill and uphold the universe even while incarnate; in fact the catholic Christological position, not a Calvinist innovation.
webster_full: EXTRA CALVINISTICUM, n. The infinite divine nature is not contained by the finite human nature. Grounded in: divine immensity (Jeremiah 23:24); Colossians 1:17 (by him all things consist); John 3:13 (the Son of man which is in heaven); Hebrews 1:3. In fact the catholic Christological position (Athanasius, Augustine, Cyril), not a Calvinist innovation. Preserves the integrity of both natures; undergirds the Reformed Supper doctrine.

corruption_summary: The extra Calvinisticum is in fact the catholic Christological position (not a Calvinist innovation); it is opposed by the Lutheran ubiquity-of-Christ's-body doctrine, which holds the divine nature so communicated its omnipresence to the human nature that Christ's body is everywhere present.
corruption_paragraphs: The extra Calvinisticum is in fact the catholic Christological position held by the Fathers and the medieval theologians, despite its name (coined polemically by Lutheran opponents). It is opposed principally by the Lutheran doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's body, developed to undergird the Lutheran consubstantiation doctrine of the Lord's Supper. The Lutheran position holds that through the communication of attributes (communicatio idiomatum) the divine attribute of omnipresence is so communicated to Christ's human nature that His body is everywhere present, enabling its bodily presence in, with, and under the elements at every celebration of the Supper. The Reformed extra Calvinisticum holds the opposite: the communication of attributes operates at the level of the Person (the one Person possesses the attributes of both natures), but the attributes of one nature are not transferred to the other nature; the divine nature retains its omnipresence and the human nature retains its finite locality; the eternal Son is united to the human nature without the human nature being made omnipresent, and continues to fill and uphold the universe according to His divine nature even while the human nature is locally embodied. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive extra Calvinisticum: the eternal Son, in the incarnation, was united to but not confined within the human nature; even while incarnate, He continued to fill and uphold the cosmos according to His divine nature (Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3); the doctrine preserves the integrity of both natures and undergirds the Reformed spiritual-presence doctrine of the Supper (Christ's body remaining in heaven, the believer's heart lifted up by the Spirit to commune with Him) against the Lutheran ubiquity doctrine.

etymology: From Greek autos (self) + theos (God): God of Himself. Calvin's emphasis that the Son, considered with respect to His deity / essence, is autotheos — God of Himself, possessing the divine essence underived and in His own right, not deriving His deity from the Father. Distinguished from the eternal generation of the Person of the Son.
biblical_def: From Greek autos (self) + theos (God), meaning God of Himself; the term associated with Calvin's emphasis that the Son, considered with respect to His deity or divine essence, is autotheos — God of Himself, possessing the one undivided divine essence underived, in His own right, in the fullest sense God. The doctrine requires careful statement to avoid both subordinationism and a denial of eternal generation. The orthodox Nicene doctrine holds that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (eternal generation), so that the Father is the eternal source or fountainhead (fons) of the Son's personal subsistence; the Son is God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God (the Nicene Creed). Calvin's autotheos emphasis clarifies and guards this: while the Person of the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (the Son derives His personal subsistence, His sonship, from the Father by eternal generation), the divine essence which the Son possesses is not begotten, derived, or communicated — the one divine essence is self-existent (a se), and the Son, possessing that one undivided self-existent essence, is in respect of His deity autotheos, God of Himself, not a lesser or derived God. The distinction is precise: the Son's personhood / sonship is from the Father (eternal generation); the Son's deity / essence is underived (autotheos). This guards against the subordinationist error that would make the Son a lesser God deriving His very deity from the Father (a step toward Arianism). Calvin's emphasis was controversial in his day but has been substantially received in the Reformed tradition as a legitimate clarification guarding the full and underived deity of the Son. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the Son is eternally begotten of the Father with respect to His Person (eternal generation), and is autotheos, God of Himself, with respect to His essence (the one self-existent divine essence, undivided and underived); the Son is fully, equally, and underivedly God, co-equal and co-eternal with the Father.

webster_full: AUTOTHEOS, n. (Trinitarian theology; Greek autos [self] + theos [God], God of Himself) Calvin's emphasis that the Son, with respect to His deity/essence, is autotheos — God of Himself, possessing the one undivided self-existent divine essence underived, in His own right. The precise distinction: the Person/sonship of the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (eternal generation; the Father the fons of the Son's personal subsistence); but the divine essence the Son possesses is not begotten or derived (the one essence is self-existent, a se). Guards against the subordinationist error that would make the Son a lesser, derived God. Received in the Reformed tradition as a legitimate clarification guarding the full and underived deity of the Son.

corruption_paragraphs: Autotheos as a doctrine requires precise statement to avoid two errors. The subordinationist error would make the Son a lesser God who derives His very deity (essence) from the Father, so that the Son is God in a secondary or derived sense; this is a step toward Arianism and contradicts the full, equal deity of the Son (John 1:1; Colossians 2:9; John 10:30). The opposite error would so emphasize the autotheos as to deny the eternal generation of the Son, collapsing the eternal relations of origin that distinguish the Persons; this contradicts the Nicene doctrine of eternal generation. Calvin's autotheos emphasis holds the precise distinction that avoids both errors: the Person of the Son is eternally begotten of the Father (eternal generation; the Son is God of God with respect to His personal subsistence), but the divine essence the Son possesses is the one self-existent, underived essence (the Son is autotheos with respect to His deity; He does not possess a lesser or derived deity). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the Son is eternally begotten of the Father as to His Person, and is God of Himself (autotheos) as to His essence; He is fully, equally, and underivedly God, co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. John 5:26 captures the balance: the Father has life in Himself, and has given to the Son to have life in Himself (the Son's having-life-in-Himself, the underived self-existence of the essence, is the Father's eternal communication of the one essence to the Son in eternal generation, such that the Son possesses the self-existent life of the one divine essence in His own right).

etymology: Also called Sabellianism (after Sabellius, 3rd century) and modalistic monarchianism. The Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons, holding that Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes, masks, or manifestations of the one God rather than three distinct co-eternal Persons.
biblical_def: Also called Sabellianism (after Sabellius, an early-third-century teacher) and modalistic monarchianism; the Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons of the Godhead. Modalism holds that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three distinct co-eternal Persons but three modes, masks (Latin personae in the theatrical sense), roles, or successive manifestations of the one God: the one God appears as Father in creation, as Son in redemption, and as Spirit in sanctification, but these are not three distinct Persons in eternal relation, only three modes of the one divine Person. The modalist denies that the Father, Son, and Spirit are eternally distinct, sometimes holding that the same divine Person who was the Father became the Son in the incarnation and then the Spirit at Pentecost (a successive modalism that produces the heresy of patripassianism — that the Father suffered on the cross, since on modalist terms the Father and the Son are the same Person). Modalism contradicts the biblical revelation of the three Persons in real, simultaneous relation to one another: the Father loves the Son (John 17:24); the Son prays to the Father (John 17); the Father sends the Son (John 3:16) and the Spirit (John 14:26); at Christ's baptism, all three Persons are simultaneously present and distinct (the Son baptized, the Spirit descending, the Father speaking from heaven, Matthew 3:16-17); the Son is with God and is God (John 1:1, distinguishing the Word from God-the-Father while affirming the Word's deity). Modalism was condemned by the early church and is rejected by all orthodox Trinitarian theology. The contemporary form is principally Oneness Pentecostalism (the United Pentecostal Church and related bodies), which denies the Trinity and holds a modalist view of God. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against modalism: God is one essence in three co-equal, co-eternal, really-distinct Persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), eternally distinguished by their personal relations, not three modes or manifestations of one Person.
webster_summary: Also Sabellianism / modalistic monarchianism; the Trinitarian heresy denying the real eternal distinction of the three Persons, holding Father, Son, and Spirit are three modes, masks, or manifestations of the one divine Person; contradicted by the simultaneous distinct presence of the Persons (Matthew 3:16-17; John 17); contemporary form Oneness Pentecostalism.
webster_full: MODALISM (ERROR), n. Successive modalism produces patripassianism (the Father suffered on the cross, the Father and Son being the same Person). Contradicted by the simultaneous distinct presence of the Persons: Christ's baptism (Son baptized, Spirit descending, Father speaking, Matthew 3:16-17); the Son praying to the Father (John 17); the Word with God and being God (John 1:1). Condemned by the early church. Contemporary form: Oneness Pentecostalism (United Pentecostal Church).

corruption_paragraphs: Modalism is the Trinitarian heresy that denies the real, eternal distinction of the three Persons. It arose in the early church (associated principally with Sabellius in the third century) as an attempt to preserve the unity of God (monotheism) and the deity of Christ while avoiding what its proponents feared was tritheism; but it did so by collapsing the three Persons into three modes or manifestations of the one divine Person. The fatal problem is that modalism cannot account for the biblical revelation of the three Persons in real, simultaneous relation to one another. At Christ's baptism, all three Persons are simultaneously present and distinct: the Son is baptized in the water, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven (Matthew 3:16-17) — three distinct Persons acting simultaneously, impossible on modalist terms. The Son prays to the Father (John 17), distinguishing the praying Son from the Father He addresses; the Son speaks of the glory He had with the Father before the world was (John 17:5), an eternal relation between two distinct Persons; the Word was with God and was God (John 1:1), distinguishing the Word from God-the-Father while affirming the Word's full deity. The successive form of modalism produces the further heresy of patripassianism (since on modalist terms the Father and the Son are the same Person, the Father suffered on the cross). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene Trinitarian doctrine against modalism: God is one essence in three co-equal, co-eternal, really-distinct Persons, eternally distinguished by their personal relations (the Father unbegotten, the Son eternally begotten, the Spirit eternally proceeding), not three modes or successive manifestations of one Person. The contemporary form of modalism is principally Oneness Pentecostalism, which denies the Trinity; the patriarchal-Reformed reader recognizes Oneness theology as a serious departure from orthodox Trinitarian Christianity.

etymology: The Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status — making the Son a lesser or derived deity rather than co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. Distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (which involve order but not inequality). Arianism is the extreme form.
biblical_def: The Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and the Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status, making the Son a lesser or derived deity rather than co-equal and co-eternal with the Father. Subordinationism comes in degrees. The extreme form is Arianism (4th century), which held that the Son is a created being, the first and highest of creatures, of a different substance from the Father (heteroousios or at most homoiousios, of like substance, but not homoousios, of the same substance); the Son had a beginning (there was when he was not), is not eternal, and is not fully God. Arianism was condemned at the Council of Nicaea (325), which affirmed the Son homoousios (of one substance) with the Father, eternally begotten, very God of very God. Milder forms of subordinationism stop short of making the Son a creature but still subordinate the Son to the Father in some respect of essence, glory, or authority. The orthodox doctrine must be carefully distinguished from subordinationism. The orthodox Nicene doctrine affirms an order (taxis) among the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin (the Father is the unbegotten source; the Son is eternally begotten of the Father; the Spirit eternally proceeds) — an order of relation and origin, but not of essence, being, glory, or status. The three Persons are co-equal and co-eternal, sharing the one undivided divine essence equally; the order of the relations does not imply any inequality. A contemporary debate concerns the eternal functional subordination of the Son (EFS / ERAS), the view (held by some complementarian theologians and contested by others) that the Son is eternally subordinate to the Father in role/function (though equal in essence); critics charge that this risks a form of subordinationism and compromises the equality of the Persons, while proponents distinguish functional from essential subordination. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene doctrine against subordinationism: the Son is co-equal and co-eternal with the Father, of one substance (homoousios), fully God; the eternal relations of origin involve order but not inequality of essence, glory, or status; and the patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the contemporary EFS debate with appropriate care, holding firmly to the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons.

webster_full: SUBORDINATIONISM (ERROR), n. Extreme form: Arianism (4th c.; the Son a created being, there was when he was not, not homoousios); condemned at Nicaea (325, the Son homoousios, eternally begotten, very God of very God). Milder forms subordinate the Son in some respect of essence, glory, or authority. Distinguished from the orthodox eternal relations of origin (an order/taxis grounded in the relations — Father unbegotten, Son begotten, Spirit proceeding — but not inequality of essence). Contemporary debate: eternal functional subordination (EFS/ERAS).

corruption_paragraphs: Subordinationism is the Trinitarian error that subordinates the Son (and Spirit) to the Father in essence, being, or eternal status. The extreme form, Arianism, made the Son a created being — the first and highest of creatures, but not eternal and not fully God (there was when he was not); this was decisively condemned at the Council of Nicaea (325), which affirmed the Son homoousios (of one substance) with the Father, eternally begotten, very God of very God. The orthodox doctrine must be carefully distinguished from subordinationism. The Nicene faith affirms an order (taxis) among the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin — the Father is the unbegotten fountainhead, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, the Spirit eternally proceeds — but this is an order of relation and origin, not of essence, glory, or status. The three Persons share the one undivided divine essence equally; they are co-equal and co-eternal; the order of the relations implies no inequality (the eternally-begotten Son is not thereby lesser than the Father, any more than a human son shares the same human nature as his father without being a lesser kind of being). A contemporary debate concerns the eternal functional subordination of the Son (EFS / ERAS), held by some complementarian theologians (who argue the Son is eternally subordinate to the Father in role while equal in essence, sometimes appealing to it as a Trinitarian ground for human gender roles) and contested by others (who charge that it risks subordinationism and compromises the equality of the Persons, and that the eternal relations of origin, not an eternal subordination of role, are the proper Nicene grounding). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Nicene doctrine against subordinationism (the Son co-equal and co-eternal, homoousios with the Father), and engages the EFS debate with appropriate care, holding firmly to the co-equality and co-eternity of the Persons grounded in the eternal relations of origin.

etymology: The doctrine that the second Person of the Trinity is and always has been the Son of God from all eternity — not becoming the Son at the incarnation or at some point in time, but eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father. Grounded in the eternal generation of the Son and the biblical witness to the Son's eternal pre-existence.
biblical_def: The doctrine that the second Person of the Trinity is and always has been the Son of God from all eternity — eternally the Son in His eternal relation to the Father, not becoming the Son at the incarnation, at the resurrection, or at any point in time. The doctrine is grounded in the eternal generation of the Son (the Son eternally begotten of the Father) and the biblical witness to the Son's eternal pre-existence and eternal filial relation to the Father. The biblical foundation: (1) the Son's eternal pre-existence and glory with the Father — the glory which I had with thee before the world was (John 17:5); before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58); the Word who was in the beginning with God and was God (John 1:1-2); (2) the Father sending the Son into the world (which presupposes the Son's existence as Son prior to His being sent) — God sent forth his Son (Galatians 4:4); God sent his only begotten Son into the world (1 John 4:9); God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (John 3:16); (3) the eternal love of the Father for the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24); (4) the Son as the eternal only begotten (monogenes) of the Father (John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). The doctrine holds that the Son's sonship is not a function of the incarnation (He did not become the Son by being born of Mary) nor of the resurrection (Romans 1:4, the declaration of His sonship with power by the resurrection, reveals rather than constitutes His eternal sonship), but is His eternal personal property — He is eternally the Son in eternal relation to the Father. The doctrine is distinguished from incarnational sonship (the minority view, held by some, that the Son became the Son at the incarnation) and from adoptionism (the heresy that Jesus was a man adopted to divine sonship). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of eternal sonship as the historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional position: the second Person of the Trinity is eternally the Son, eternally begotten of the Father, in eternal filial relation; He did not become the Son but is and ever was the Son; the incarnation is the eternal Son's taking of human nature, not the beginning of His sonship.

webster_full: ETERNAL SONSHIP, n. phr. Distinguished from incarnational sonship and adoptionism. The historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional position.

corruption_paragraphs: Eternal sonship is the historic orthodox and Reformed-confessional doctrine, held against two positions. Adoptionism (an early heresy, recurring in various forms) holds that Jesus was a man who was adopted to divine sonship at some point (His baptism, His resurrection); this contradicts the biblical revelation of the Son's eternal pre-existence and deity (John 1:1; 17:5) and is a form of denying the true deity of Christ. Incarnational sonship (a minority view held by some orthodox theologians, notably advocated for a time by certain evangelical figures) holds that the second Person of the Trinity became the Son at the incarnation — eternally the Word or the second Person, but becoming the Son only when He took human nature; this view, while not heretical in the way adoptionism is (it affirms the eternal deity and pre-existence of the second Person), is rejected by the historic orthodox and Reformed tradition as failing to account for the biblical witness to the Son's eternal filial relation to the Father (the Father loving the Son before the foundation of the world, John 17:24; the Father sending the Son, which presupposes His prior sonship, Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:9). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of eternal sonship: the second Person of the Trinity is eternally the Son, eternally begotten of the Father, in eternal filial relation; He did not become the Son but is and ever was the Son; the incarnation is the eternal Son's taking of human nature, not the beginning of His sonship. This doctrine guards the eternal relations of the Trinity (the Father eternally Father, the Son eternally Son) and undergirds the gospel's revelation of the Father's eternal love displayed in sending His eternal Son (John 3:16).

etymology: The doctrine that Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, without a human father. Grounded in the prophecy of Isaiah 7:14 and the narratives of Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:26-38. One of the fundamentals of the faith.
biblical_def: The doctrine that Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, without a human father — that Mary conceived and bore the Son while remaining a virgin, the conception being a supernatural work of the Holy Spirit. The doctrine is grounded in the prophecy and the Gospel narratives: (1) Isaiah 7:14, Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (the Hebrew almah, rendered parthenos, virgin, in the Septuagint and cited as fulfilled in Matthew 1:23); (2) Matthew 1:18-25, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost... that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost; Joseph knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son; (3) Luke 1:26-38, Gabriel's announcement to Mary, her question How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?, and the angel's answer, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God. The theological significance of the virgin birth: (1) it marks the supernatural entrance of the eternal Son into human nature (the incarnation accomplished by the Holy Spirit's miraculous work, not by ordinary generation); (2) it is connected to the sinlessness of Christ (the holy thing born of Mary, conceived by the Spirit, free from the entail of original sin transmitted through ordinary generation, though the precise mechanism is debated); (3) it fulfills the prophetic promise of the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15, the woman's seed, not the man's) and the Immanuel prophecy (Isaiah 7:14). The virgin birth was affirmed in the early creeds (conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary, the Apostles' Creed) and is one of the fundamentals of the faith (one of the five fundamentals defended by the early-twentieth-century fundamentalists against liberal denial). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the virgin birth against the liberal-Protestant denial (which dismisses it as legend or myth) and the rationalist rejection of the miraculous; the virgin birth is a historical fact attested by the inspired Gospel narratives, a fundamental of the faith, and the marvelous manner of the eternal Son's entrance into human nature.

corruption_paragraphs: The virgin birth is held against the liberal-Protestant denial and the rationalist rejection of the miraculous. Liberal Protestantism (from the 19th-century higher criticism onward) commonly dismisses the virgin birth as a legendary or mythological accretion, a pious fiction not to be taken as historical fact; this denial was one of the marks of the modernist theology that the early-twentieth-century fundamentalists opposed (the virgin birth being one of the five fundamentals). The doctrine is theologically significant: it marks the supernatural manner of the eternal Son's entrance into human nature (the incarnation accomplished by the Holy Spirit's miraculous work); it is connected to the sinlessness of Christ; and it fulfills the prophetic promise of the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15) and the Immanuel prophecy. The believer confesses with the historic church that the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary — the marvelous manner of the incarnation, by which the eternal Son took human nature in the womb of the virgin, God manifest in the flesh.

etymology: The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the two states of the Mediator: the state of humiliation (Christ's condescension in His incarnation, suffering, death, and burial) and the state of exaltation (His resurrection, ascension, session at the Father's right hand, and return in glory). Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56.
biblical_def: The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the two states of the Mediator: the state of humiliation and the state of exaltation, describing the two great phases of Christ's mediatorial work. The doctrine is grounded principally in Philippians 2:5-11 (the Christ-hymn, descending into humiliation and ascending into exaltation) and codified in the Reformed confessions (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56). The state of humiliation comprises Christ's condescension and the lowliness He endured for our salvation: His incarnation (taking our nature, born in a low condition); His subjection to the law; His enduring the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; His being buried and continuing under the power of death for a time (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27, Christ's humiliation consisted in his being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time). The state of exaltation comprises Christ's glorification: His resurrection from the dead on the third day; His ascension into heaven; His sitting at the right hand of God the Father; and His coming to judge the world at the last day (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 28, Christ's exaltation consisteth in his rising again from the dead on the third day, in ascending up into heaven, in sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and in coming to judge the world at the last day). The two states correspond to the descent and ascent of Philippians 2: the eternal Son descended into the depths of humiliation (emptying Himself, taking the form of a servant, humbling Himself unto death, even the death of the cross) and was then exalted to the heights (God highly exalted Him and gave Him a name above every name). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the two states as a comprehensive framework for the mediatorial work of Christ: the humiliation by which He accomplished redemption (descending to bear our guilt and curse) and the exaltation by which He was vindicated and now reigns (ascending to His glory and rule); the believer's salvation rests on both — redeemed by the humiliation, and saved to the uttermost by the living, reigning, interceding, returning, exalted Christ.

webster_full: STATES OF CHRIST (HUMILIATION AND EXALTATION), n. phr. (Christology) The two states of the Mediator. Grounded in Philippians 2:5-11; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q. 27-28; Larger Catechism Q. 46-56. Humiliation (Q. 27): being born in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; being buried and continuing under the power of death for a time. Exaltation (Q. 28): rising again on the third day, ascending into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and coming to judge the world at the last day. The descent and ascent of Philippians 2: the Son descended into humiliation (emptying Himself, the form of a servant, obedient unto death) and was exalted to the heights (a name above every name).

corruption_summary: The two states of Christ are the comprehensive framework for His mediatorial work; the principal mishandling is the neglect of one state — emphasizing the humiliation (the suffering Savior) while neglecting the exaltation (the reigning Lord), or vice versa.
corruption_paragraphs: States of Christ as a doctrine does not undergo lexical corruption. The principal mishandling is the neglect of one state at the expense of the other. Some traditions and spiritualities emphasize the humiliation of Christ (the suffering Savior, the crucified Christ, the man of sorrows) while neglecting the exaltation (the risen, ascended, reigning, returning Lord); this can produce a Christianity fixated on the cross and the suffering Christ without the triumphant note of the resurrection, ascension, and reign. Others emphasize the exaltation (the glorious reigning Christ, the triumphant King) while neglecting the humiliation (the depths of suffering by which He accomplished redemption); this can produce a triumphalism that loses sight of the cross. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of the two states in their fulness: the humiliation by which Christ accomplished redemption (descending to bear our guilt, endure the wrath of God, die the cursed death of the cross, and continue under death's power for a time) and the exaltation by which He was vindicated and now reigns (rising from the dead, ascending to heaven, sitting at the Father's right hand, and returning to judge the world). Both states are essential to the gospel and to the believer's salvation: he is redeemed by the humiliation of Christ (the crucified Savior who bore his sins) and saved to the uttermost by the exaltation of Christ (the living, reigning, interceding, returning Lord). Luke 24:26 holds the two together: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? — the suffering (humiliation) and the glory (exaltation) are the two great phases of the one mediatorial work.

etymology: From Latin mediator (one who stands between, a go-between); Greek mesites (1 Timothy 2:5). The doctrine that Christ is the one Mediator between God and men, the God-man who reconciles God and fallen humanity through His mediatorial work in His threefold office.
biblical_def: From Latin mediator (one who stands between); Greek mesites; the doctrine that Christ is the one and only Mediator between God and men, the God-man who reconciles God and fallen humanity through His mediatorial work. The foundational text: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; Who gave himself a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5-6). The doctrine of Christ as Mediator. (1) The necessity of a mediator: fallen man, alienated from the holy God by sin and under His just wrath, cannot approach God directly or reconcile himself; a mediator is needed to stand between the offended God and the offending sinner, to reconcile the two. (2) The qualifications of the Mediator: only the God-man could mediate — as God, He has infinite worth and access to God; as man, He represents men and stands in their place; uniting both natures in His one Person, He alone can lay His hand upon both God and man (the longing of Job 9:33, neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both, answered in Christ). (3) The mediatorial work: Christ mediates in His threefold office (prophet, priest, king), supremely as Priest, offering Himself as the ransom and interceding for His people; He is the Mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 9:15; 12:24), the surety of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22), through whom alone we have access to the Father (John 14:6, no man cometh unto the Father, but by me; Ephesians 2:18). (4) The exclusivity of the Mediator: there is ONE Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5); Christ alone mediates between God and men; no other mediator — not Mary, not the saints, not angels, not priests in the Roman sense — stands between God and men. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of Christ the one Mediator against the Roman Catholic system of secondary mediators (the intercession of Mary and the saints, the mediatorial priesthood) and against every attempt to approach God apart from Christ. There is one God and one Mediator, the man Christ Jesus; through Him alone the sinner is reconciled to God and has access to the Father; He is the all-sufficient, exclusive, and only Mediator of the covenant of grace.
webster_summary: From Greek mesites; the doctrine that Christ is the one Mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), the God-man who reconciles God and fallen humanity through His mediatorial work in His threefold office; the exclusive Mediator against the Roman system of secondary mediators (Mary, the saints, the priesthood).
webster_full: MEDIATOR (DOCTRINE), n. (Christology / soteriology; Latin mediator; Greek mesites) Christ is the one and only Mediator between God and men. Foundation: 1 Timothy 2:5-6 (one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom). (1) Necessity: fallen man cannot approach the holy God or reconcile himself; a mediator is needed. (2) Qualifications: only the God-man could mediate (as God, infinite worth and access; as man, representing men; uniting both, He lays His hand on both, Job 9:33). (3) Work: mediates in His threefold office, supremely as Priest; Mediator of the new covenant (Hebrews 9:15; 12:24); access to the Father through Him alone (John 14:6). (4) Exclusivity: ONE Mediator; no other (not Mary, the saints, angels, or priests). Held against the Roman system of secondary mediators.

corruption_summary: Christ is the one and exclusive Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5); the principal corruption is the Roman Catholic system of secondary mediators (the intercession of Mary and the saints, the mediatorial priesthood) that interposes other mediators between God and men.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine of Christ as the one Mediator is held principally against the Roman Catholic system of secondary mediators. Roman Catholic theology and practice interpose other mediators between God and men: the intercession of Mary (invoked as Mediatrix and co-redemptrix in popular and some official Catholic devotion); the intercession of the saints (prayers addressed to the saints, who are held to intercede with God on the petitioner's behalf); and the mediatorial priesthood (the Catholic priest as a mediator who offers the sacrifice of the mass and dispenses grace through the sacraments). The biblical doctrine is emphatic: there is ONE Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5); the exclusivity is the point of the verse (one God, one Mediator). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: Christ alone is the Mediator; through Him alone the sinner is reconciled to God; through Him alone the believer has access to the Father (John 14:6; Ephesians 2:18; Hebrews 4:14-16, coming boldly to the throne of grace through our great High Priest); no other mediator — not Mary, not the saints, not angels, not any human priest — stands between God and men. The believer prays directly to God through Christ the one Mediator, needing no secondary intercessor; the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9) means every believer has direct access to God through the one Mediator. The exclusivity and all-sufficiency of Christ's mediation is a precious gospel truth: the believer comes to God not through a hierarchy of secondary mediators but directly through the one Mediator, the God-man Christ Jesus, who ever lives to make intercession for him (Hebrews 7:25).

etymology: From Greek dyo (two) + thelema (will); the orthodox doctrine, defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), that Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures. Opposed to monothelitism (the heresy that Christ has only one will).
biblical_def: From Greek dyo (two) + thelema (will); the orthodox Christological doctrine that Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures, the human will being in perfect, unconfused submission to and harmony with the divine will. The doctrine was defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681, the Sixth Ecumenical Council) against the heresy of monothelitism (from monos, one, + thelema, will), which held that Christ has only one will. The logic of dyothelitism follows from the two-natures doctrine of Chalcedon: a complete human nature includes a human will (the will being a faculty of the nature, not merely of the person); therefore the complete human nature of Christ includes a complete human will, distinct from His divine will; Christ has two wills, corresponding to His two natures. The biblical foundation is principally the agony in Gethsemane, where Christ's human will and the divine will are distinctly expressed yet in perfect harmony: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt (Matthew 26:39; cf. Luke 22:42, not my will, but thine, be done). The distinction between my will (the human will of Christ, naturally recoiling from the cup of suffering and wrath) and thy will (the divine will, to which the human will perfectly submits) displays the two wills in their distinct operation and perfect harmony. Dyothelitism guards the integrity and completeness of Christ's human nature (a human nature without a human will would be incomplete, and the redemption of the human will would be unaccomplished, on the principle that what is not assumed is not healed). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine of dyothelitism: Christ has two wills, divine and human, corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect submission to and harmony with the divine; this preserves the completeness of His humanity (including the redemption of the human will, displayed in Gethsemane's not my will, but thine, be done) and the integrity of the two-natures Christology.

webster_full: DYOTHELITISM, n. (Christology; Greek dyo [two] + thelema [will]) Christ has two wills — a divine will and a human will — corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect, unconfused submission to and harmony with the divine. Defined at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681, Sixth Ecumenical Council) against monothelitism (one will). The logic follows from Chalcedon: a complete human nature includes a human will (a faculty of the nature); Christ's complete human nature includes a human will distinct from His divine will. Biblical foundation: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39, not as I will, but as thou wilt; Luke 22:42, not my will, but thine, be done). Guards the completeness of Christ's humanity (what is not assumed is not healed).

corruption_paragraphs: Dyothelitism is held against the heresy of monothelitism (one will in Christ). Monothelitism arose in the seventh century as an attempt at compromise with the monophysites (who held one nature in Christ); it conceded two natures but held that Christ has only one will (a single divine-human will, or a will belonging only to the divine Person). The orthodox church rejected monothelitism at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) on the substantive ground that it compromises the completeness of Christ's human nature: the will is a faculty of the nature (not merely of the person), so that a complete human nature must include a complete human will; a Christ with only one will would lack a complete human nature, and the redemption of the human will (which fell in Adam and must be redeemed in Christ) would be unaccomplished — on the patristic principle that what is not assumed is not healed (Gregory of Nazianzus), the human will must be assumed by Christ to be redeemed. The biblical foundation for dyothelitism is principally the agony in Gethsemane, where Christ's human will and the divine will are distinctly expressed yet in perfect harmony: not my will, but thine, be done (Luke 22:42). The distinction between Christ's human will (naturally recoiling from the cup of suffering) and the divine will (to which the human will perfectly submits) displays the two wills. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive orthodox doctrine: Christ has two wills, divine and human, corresponding to His two natures, the human will in perfect submission to and harmony with the divine; this preserves the completeness of His humanity and the integrity of the two-natures Christology, and displays the perfect obedience of the incarnate Son, whose human will, though it naturally shrank from the cross, perfectly submitted to the Father's will for our redemption.

etymology: From Greek en (in) + hypostasis (person). The Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is personalized in (enhypostatized by) the divine Person. biblical_def: From Greek en (in) + hypostasis (person, subsistence); the Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is personalized in (enhypostatized by) the divine Person of the Word. The doctrine, developed principally by Leontius of Byzantium (6th century) and refined in subsequent Christology, addresses a precise question raised by the two-natures doctrine: in what person does the human nature of Christ subsist? The answer is paired in two terms. Anhypostasia (from an-, without, + hypostasis): the human nature of Christ has no independent personhood of its own — it never existed as a separate human person; there is no human person of Jesus alongside the divine Person. Enhypostasia (from en-, in): the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is real and complete (a true human nature, body and reasonable soul) but is personalized in the divine Person, never having a separate personhood. The two terms together express the orthodox doctrine: the human nature of Christ is complete but not independently personal; it subsists in and is personalized by the Person of the Word; there are not two persons (against Nestorianism) but one Person (the eternal Son) subsisting in two natures, the human nature being enhypostatic (personalized in the divine Person). This guards against two errors: Nestorianism (which would make the human nature an independent person, producing two persons in Christ) and the supposition that the human nature is impersonal in the sense of being incomplete or sub-human. The human nature is fully and completely human (lacking nothing proper to humanity except sin) but is personalized in the divine Person of the Son rather than constituting a separate human person. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of enhypostasia (with anhypostasia): the human nature of Christ is real, complete, and personalized in the Person of the eternal Son; there is one Person (the Word) subsisting in two natures, the human nature having its personal subsistence in the divine Person; this preserves the unity of Christ's Person (against Nestorianism) and the completeness of His human nature (against the incompleteness errors).

etymology: From Greek an- (without) + hypostasis (person). The Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has no independent personhood of its own — it never existed as a separate human person apart from its union with the Word. biblical_def: From Greek an- (without) + hypostasis (person, subsistence); the Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has no independent personhood of its own — it never existed as a separate human person apart from its union with the eternal Word. The doctrine is the negative counterpart to enhypostasia (the positive doctrine that the human nature subsists in the Person of the Son), and the two must be held together. Anhypostasia denies that there is a separate human person of Jesus alongside the divine Person of the Word: the human nature of Christ did not exist for a moment as an independent human person before being assumed; it never had, and does not have, a personhood of its own; from the moment of its conception by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin, the human nature was assumed into union with the Person of the Word and personalized in Him. This guards the unity of Christ's Person against Nestorianism. But anhypostasia must be balanced by enhypostasia (lest it imply that the human nature is impersonal in the sense of incomplete or unreal): the human nature, though having no independent personhood, is not impersonal or incomplete; it has its personal subsistence in the Person of the Son (enhypostasia). The two terms together express the orthodox doctrine: the human nature of Christ is real and complete (a true human nature, body and reasonable soul, lacking nothing proper to humanity except sin) but is not independently personal (anhypostasia); rather, it is personalized in the divine Person of the Word (enhypostasia). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of anhypostasia (with enhypostasia): the human nature of Christ never existed as a separate human person but was assumed from its conception into union with the Person of the eternal Son, personalized in Him; there is one Person (the Word) subsisting in two natures; this preserves the unity of Christ's Person (against Nestorianism, which would produce two persons) while the paired enhypostasia preserves the reality and completeness of the human nature.
