etymology: The Christological doctrine, drawn principally from the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-18), that the eternal Son is the Logos (Word) of God — eternally with God and eternally God, the agent of creation, and the one who became flesh in the incarnation. Greek logos (word, reason, account).
biblical_def: The Christological doctrine, drawn principally from the prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1-18), that the eternal Son is the Logos (Word) of God. The Greek logos means word, reason, account, or rational principle; John takes the term (which had rich background in both Hebrew thought — the creative Word of God, the dabar YHWH — and Greek philosophy — the logos as the rational principle of the cosmos) and applies it to the eternal Son. The Johannine prologue establishes the foundational Logos Christology: (1) the eternal pre-existence of the Word — In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1a; the Word already existed in the beginning, before creation); (2) the distinct personhood of the Word in relation to God — and the Word was with God (John 1:1b; the Word in eternal relation with God-the-Father, distinct from Him); (3) the full deity of the Word — and the Word was God (John 1:1c; the Word is fully God, of the same divine essence); (4) the Word as the agent of creation — All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3; the Word as the divine agent through whom all things were created; cf. Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2); (5) the incarnation of the Word — And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (John 1:14; the eternal Word took human nature, the incarnation). The Logos Christology grounds the eternal deity, pre-existence, distinct personhood, creative agency, and incarnation of the Son. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Logos Christology of John's prologue against the various denials: the Arian denial (which would make the Logos a created being); the modalist denial (which would deny the Word's distinct personhood); and the liberal reduction (which would treat the Logos as a mere abstraction or principle rather than the eternal personal Son). The Logos who was in the beginning, who was with God, who was God, by whom all things were made, was made flesh and dwelt among us — this is the foundational Christology of John's prologue and the Reformed-confessional doctrine of the eternal Son who became incarnate for our salvation.

webster_full: LOGOS CHRISTOLOGY, n. phr. (Christology; Greek logos, word, reason, account) The eternal Son is the Logos (Word) of God, drawn principally from John 1:1-18. John takes the term (rich in Hebrew background — the creative dabar YHWH — and Greek philosophy) and applies it to the eternal Son. The prologue: eternal pre-existence (In the beginning was the Word, 1:1a); distinct personhood (the Word was with God, 1:1b); full deity (the Word was God, 1:1c); agent of creation (all things were made by him, 1:3); incarnation (the Word was made flesh, 1:14). Grounds the eternal deity, pre-existence, distinct personhood, creative agency, and incarnation of the Son. Held against Arianism, modalism, and the liberal reduction of the Logos to an abstraction.

corruption_summary: The Logos Christology of John's prologue grounds the eternal deity, pre-existence, and incarnation of the Son; held against Arianism (the Logos a creature), modalism (denying the Word's distinct personhood), and the liberal reduction of the Logos to a mere abstraction.
corruption_paragraphs: The Logos Christology of John's prologue is held against several denials. The Arian denial would make the Logos a created being (the highest creature, but not eternal and not fully God); this contradicts John 1:1c (the Word was God) and John 1:1a (In the beginning was the Word, the Word already existing before creation, not Himself created). The modalist denial would deny the distinct personhood of the Word (treating the Word as merely a mode of the one God); this contradicts John 1:1b (the Word was with God, the Word in distinct relation with God-the-Father). The liberal reduction would treat the Logos as a mere abstraction, principle, or impersonal divine reason rather than the eternal personal Son; this contradicts the prologue's clear presentation of the Word as a distinct Person (with God, made flesh, beholding His glory) who became incarnate. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Logos Christology: the eternal Son is the Logos, the Word of God, who was in the beginning, who was with God (distinct personhood), who was God (full deity), by whom all things were made (creative agency), and who was made flesh and dwelt among us (incarnation). The Johannine prologue is one of the great foundational texts of orthodox Christology, establishing the eternal deity, pre-existence, distinct personhood, creative agency, and incarnation of the Son. The believer beholds in the incarnate Logos the glory of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14), and confesses the eternal Word who became flesh for the salvation of His people.

etymology: Greek Theotokos (God-bearer, often rendered Mother of God). The Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius, who preferred Christotokos (Christ-bearer). The debate was substantively Christological (the unity of Christ's Person), not primarily Mariological.
biblical_def: Greek Theotokos (literally God-bearer, often rendered Mother of God); the Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius. The debate was substantively Christological, not primarily Mariological — it concerned the unity of Christ's Person, not the exaltation of Mary. Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, objected to the term Theotokos and preferred Christotokos (Christ-bearer), on the ground that Mary bore the human nature of Christ, not His divine nature (and God, being eternal, cannot be born); Nestorius's underlying Christology so divided the two natures as to imply two persons in Christ (a divine person and a human person), so that Mary bore the human person/nature but not the divine. Cyril of Alexandria and the Council of Ephesus affirmed Theotokos on the substantive Christological ground that the one Person born of Mary is the eternal Son of God: because Christ is one Person (not two), and that Person is the divine Son who took human nature, the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son (in His incarnate state); Mary is therefore rightly called Theotokos (God-bearer) — not because she is the source of Christ's deity (she is not; the Son is eternally God) or the mother of the divine nature (the divine nature is not born), but because the one Person she bore is truly God the Son incarnate. The term affirms the unity of Christ's Person (one Person, the divine Son, born of Mary) against the Nestorian division into two persons. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Christological point affirmed by Theotokos (the unity of Christ's Person; the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son incarnate) while exercising appropriate Protestant caution about the term's later Mariological developments. The Reformers generally accepted the term Theotokos in its proper Christological sense (Calvin affirmed it could be used rightly, though he was wary of its potential abuse) while rejecting the Roman Catholic Marian dogmas (the immaculate conception, the assumption, the co-redemptrix and mediatrix titles) that developed around the exaltation of Mary. The substantive point is Christological: the one Person born of the virgin is the eternal Son of God; the proper use of Theotokos guards the unity of Christ's Person, not the exaltation of Mary.

webster_full: THEOTOKOS (DEBATE), n. (Christology; Greek God-bearer, Mother of God) The Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius (who preferred Christotokos, Christ-bearer). Nestorius objected on the ground that Mary bore Christ's human nature, not His divine; his underlying Christology so divided the two natures as to imply two persons. Cyril of Alexandria and Ephesus affirmed Theotokos because the one Person born of Mary is the eternal Son: Christ is one Person (the divine Son who took human nature), so the one Mary bore is truly God the Son incarnate — not the source of His deity, but the one Person born is God the Son. Affirms the unity of Christ's Person against Nestorian division. The Reformers accepted it in its proper Christological sense while rejecting the later Marian dogmas.

corruption_paragraphs: The Theotokos debate must be understood as substantively Christological, not primarily Mariological — and herein lies both its proper use and its potential abuse. The original debate at Ephesus (431) concerned the unity of Christ's Person: Nestorius's preference for Christotokos over Theotokos reflected a Christology that so divided the two natures as to imply two persons in Christ (a divine person and a separate human person), so that Mary bore the human person but not God; Cyril and the Council affirmed Theotokos to defend the unity of Christ's Person (the one born of Mary is truly the eternal Son incarnate, one Person in two natures). In its proper Christological sense, Theotokos affirms a true and important point: the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son (in His incarnate state), so that Mary is rightly the mother of the Lord (Luke 1:43, Elizabeth calls Mary the mother of my Lord). The Reformers generally accepted the term in this proper Christological sense (Calvin allowed it could be rightly used, while warning against its abuse). The abuse comes when Theotokos is detached from its Christological mooring and pressed into the service of the exaltation of Mary — the later Roman Catholic Marian dogmas (the immaculate conception of Mary, her bodily assumption, her titles as co-redemptrix and mediatrix, the devotion and prayers addressed to her) that go far beyond the biblical witness and compromise the unique mediation of Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Christological point (the one born of Mary is truly God the Son incarnate; the unity of Christ's Person) while rejecting the Marian dogmas and devotion that the term has been abused to support. The proper use of Theotokos guards Christology (the unity of Christ's Person); its abuse exalts Mary beyond her biblical place.

etymology: The doctrine that Jesus Christ was entirely without sin — free from original sin and from any actual sin in thought, word, or deed throughout His life. Grounded in the explicit biblical testimony (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). Essential to His atoning work as the spotless sacrifice.
biblical_def: The doctrine that Jesus Christ was entirely without sin — free from original sin (the corruption and guilt inherited from Adam) and from any actual sin (in thought, word, or deed) throughout His life. The sinlessness of Christ is grounded in explicit and abundant biblical testimony: (1) Hebrews 4:15, He was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin; (2) 2 Corinthians 5:21, He knew no sin; (3) 1 Peter 2:22, Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth; (4) 1 John 3:5, in him is no sin; (5) Hebrews 7:26, He is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners; (6) John 8:46, His own challenge, Which of you convinceth me of sin?; (7) John 8:29, I do always those things that please him; (8) the testimony of those who examined Him (Pilate, Luke 23:4; the centurion, Luke 23:47; the dying thief, Luke 23:41). The sinlessness of Christ has two dimensions: He was free from original sin (the virgin birth being connected to this — conceived by the Holy Spirit, the holy thing born of Mary, Luke 1:35, free from the entail of Adam's corruption) and free from all actual sin (He never sinned in thought, word, or deed; He perfectly kept the law of God; His was a life of perfect, sinless obedience). The sinlessness of Christ is essential to His atoning work: as the spotless Lamb of God (1 Peter 1:19, a lamb without blemish and without spot; the OT sacrificial requirement of an unblemished victim), He alone could be the acceptable sacrifice for the sins of others; a sinful Christ would have had to die for His own sins and could not have borne the sins of others. His sinlessness is also the basis of His active obedience (the perfect law-keeping that is imputed to the believer as his righteousness). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of Christ's sinlessness against any denial or diminution; the sinless Christ, the spotless Lamb, alone could accomplish redemption, bearing our sins in His sinless body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24) and providing the perfect righteousness imputed to His people.
webster_summary: The doctrine that Jesus Christ was entirely without sin — free from original sin and from all actual sin in thought, word, or deed; Hebrews 4:15 (without sin), 2 Corinthians 5:21 (knew no sin), 1 Peter 2:22 (did no sin), 1 John 3:5 (in him is no sin); essential to His atoning work as the spotless Lamb.
webster_full: SINLESSNESS OF CHRIST, n. phr. (Christology) Jesus Christ was entirely without sin — free from original sin (the corruption and guilt inherited from Adam) and from all actual sin (in thought, word, or deed) throughout His life. Testimony: Hebrews 4:15 (tempted like as we are, yet without sin); 2 Corinthians 5:21 (knew no sin); 1 Peter 2:22 (did no sin); 1 John 3:5 (in him is no sin); Hebrews 7:26 (holy, harmless, undefiled); John 8:46 (which of you convinceth me of sin?). Free from original sin (connected to the virgin birth, Luke 1:35) and from all actual sin (perfect law-keeping). Essential to His atoning work as the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19); the basis of His active obedience imputed to the believer.

corruption_paragraphs: The sinlessness of Christ is held against any denial or diminution. The liberal-Protestant portrayal of a fallible, merely-human Jesus who shared the moral imperfections of humanity denies His sinlessness and undermines the entire structure of the atonement; this contradicts the explicit and abundant biblical testimony (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). A related question is the debate over the peccability or impeccability of Christ (whether the sinless Christ was able to sin, even though He did not, or was unable to sin); the Reformed tradition generally holds the impeccability of Christ (He was not able to sin, given the union of His human nature with the divine Person, though His temptations were nonetheless real), while affirming that in all cases He was actually sinless. The substantive point, held across the Reformed tradition, is that Christ was entirely sinless — free from original sin and from all actual sin. The sinlessness of Christ is essential to His atoning work on two grounds: (1) as the spotless Lamb of God (1 Peter 1:19; the OT requirement of an unblemished sacrificial victim), only the sinless Christ could be the acceptable sacrifice for the sins of others — a sinful Christ would have had to die for His own sins and could not have borne the sins of others; (2) the active obedience of Christ (His perfect, sinless law-keeping) is imputed to the believer as his righteousness — a Christ who had sinned would have no perfect righteousness to impute. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the sinless Christ, the spotless Lamb, who knew no sin and did no sin, in whom is no sin, alone could accomplish redemption — bearing our sins in His own sinless body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), made sin for us though He knew no sin, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him (2 Corinthians 5:21).
